title: Inflation
description: Class 12 Economics: meaning and types of inflation, demand-pull and cost-push causes, the effects of inflation on different groups, and monetary, fiscal and supply-side control measures.

topics.title: Meaning and Types of Inflation
topics.concept:
Inflation is a sustained (continuing) rise in the general price level of an economy over a period of time. The key words are "sustained" (a one-off rise is not inflation) and "general" (the average of all prices, not just one good). When prices rise, the purchasing power of money falls — the same money buys fewer goods than before. The rate of inflation is measured by a price index such as the CPI or the WPI.

Inflation is classified by its speed:

  • Creeping inflation — a slow, mild rise (low single-digit). It is generally considered harmless or even mildly good for growth.
  • Galloping (running) inflation — a rapid rise (high, often double or triple digit). It seriously harms the economy.
  • Hyperinflation — an extremely rapid, out-of-control rise where money loses its value almost daily. It can destroy a currency.

The opposite situations are also named: deflation (a sustained fall in the general price level), disinflation (a slowing of the inflation rate, prices still rising but more slowly), and stagflation (the difficult case of high inflation together with stagnation/unemployment). So inflation is essentially about money losing value as prices rise, and its severity ranges from a gentle creep to a destructive hyperinflation.

examples.solution:
Sustained, general price rise.

  • A sustained rise in the general price level over time.
  • It reduces the purchasing power of money.
examples.answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the three types of inflation by speed.
examples.solution:
From slow to runaway.

  • Creeping (mild), galloping (rapid), hyperinflation (out of control).
examples.answer: Creeping (mild), galloping (rapid) and hyperinflation (extremely rapid, out of control).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the difference between deflation and disinflation?
examples.solution:
Falling vs slowing.

  • Deflation: a sustained fall in the general price level.
  • Disinflation: a slowing of the inflation rate (prices still rising, but more slowly).
examples.answer: Deflation is a fall in the general price level; disinflation is a slowing of the inflation rate (prices still rise, but more slowly).

recap:
• Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level → purchasing power of money falls; measured by CPI/WPI.
  • By speed: creeping (mild), galloping (rapid), hyperinflation (out of control).
  • Related: deflation (price fall), disinflation (slowing inflation), stagflation (inflation + stagnation).

quiz.q: Inflation is a sustained rise in the:
quiz.explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level.

quiz.q: An extremely rapid, out-of-control price rise is:
quiz.explanation: Hyperinflation is an extremely rapid, out-of-control rise.

topics.title: Causes and Effects of Inflation
topics.concept:
Inflation has two broad causes, named after the side of the market that pushes prices up:

  • Demand-pull inflation — caused by too much demand. When aggregate demand exceeds the economy's capacity to produce (an inflationary gap), buyers compete for limited goods and pull prices up. Causes include a rise in money supply, higher government spending, easy credit, or rising incomes — in short, "too much money chasing too few goods."
  • Cost-push inflation — caused by rising costs of production. When the cost of inputs goes up — higher wages, dearer raw materials, higher oil prices, or new taxes — producers raise their prices to cover the cost, pushing the price level up even without extra demand.

The effects of inflation fall unevenly on different groups, so inflation redistributes income:

  • Who loses: people on fixed incomes (pensioners, salaried workers), lenders/creditors (they are repaid in money worth less), and savers holding cash. Their real income and savings shrink.
  • Who gains: borrowers/debtors (they repay in cheaper money), businessmen and traders (prices and profits rise), and those holding real assets (land, gold) whose value rises.

Mild inflation may even encourage production, but high inflation harms the economy: it discourages saving, creates uncertainty, hurts the poor most, and can make exports less competitive. This uneven impact is why governments work hard to keep inflation low and stable.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation?
examples.solution:
Demand side vs cost side.

  • Demand-pull: too much demand pulls prices up (too much money chasing too few goods).
  • Cost-push: rising production costs push prices up.
examples.answer: Demand-pull inflation is caused by excess demand; cost-push inflation is caused by rising production costs.

examples.problem: Example 2: Does inflation hurt a lender or a borrower more? Why?
examples.solution:
Money is worth less when repaid.

  • It hurts the lender: he is repaid in money worth less than he lent.
  • The borrower gains: he repays in cheaper money.
examples.answer: It hurts the lender, who is repaid in money worth less; the borrower gains by repaying in cheaper money.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does inflation hurt people on fixed incomes?
examples.solution:
Income does not rise with prices.

  • Their money income stays the same while prices rise.
  • So the same income buys fewer goods — their real income falls.
examples.answer: Because their fixed money income buys fewer goods as prices rise, so their real income (purchasing power) falls.

recap:
• Demand-pull inflation: excess demand ("too much money chasing too few goods"). Cost-push inflation: rising input costs (wages, oil, raw materials, taxes).
  • Inflation redistributes income: lose — fixed-income earners, lenders, savers; gain — borrowers, businessmen, holders of real assets.

quiz.q: 'Too much money chasing too few goods' describes:
quiz.explanation: Excess demand causing inflation is demand-pull inflation.
Borrowers gain because they repay loans in money worth less.

topics.title: Control Measures of Inflation
topics.concept:
Because high inflation harms the economy, the government and the central bank use several measures to control it, grouped into three kinds.

  • Monetary measures (by the RBI) — the central bank reduces the money supply and credit to curb demand. It raises the repo rate, the CRR and the SLR, and sells government securities (open market operations). Costlier and scarcer credit reduces spending, cooling demand-pull inflation. This is contractionary monetary policy.
  • Fiscal measures (by the government) — the government reduces aggregate demand through its budget: it cuts public spending and/or raises taxes, and tries to reduce the budget deficit. Lower government spending and higher taxes leave less money to be spent, reducing demand.
  • Supply-side / other measures — since inflation also comes from a shortage of goods, the government tries to increase supply: importing scarce goods, releasing buffer stocks of food, improving production and distribution, and controlling hoarding and black-marketing. Administrative measures like a public distribution system (ration shops) and price controls also help protect the poor.

The right cure depends on the cause: demand-pull inflation is best fought by reducing demand (tight monetary and fiscal policy), while cost-push inflation is best fought by easing costs and raising supply. In practice, governments use a combination. Keeping inflation low and stable — without choking growth — is one of the central goals of macroeconomic policy, completing our study of how the whole economy is managed.

examples.problem: Example 1: State two monetary measures to control inflation.
examples.solution:
The RBI tightens credit.

  • Raise the repo rate and the CRR (also raise SLR, sell securities).
examples.answer: Raising the repo rate and the cash reserve ratio (CRR) — also raising the SLR and selling government securities.

examples.problem: Example 2: What fiscal measures help control inflation?
examples.solution:
Reduce demand via the budget.

  • Cut public spending and raise taxes (reduce the deficit).
examples.answer: Cutting public expenditure and raising taxes (reducing the budget deficit) to lower aggregate demand.

examples.problem: Example 3: How can increasing the supply of goods control inflation?
examples.solution:
More goods ease prices.

  • Importing scarce goods, releasing buffer stocks, and curbing hoarding raise supply.
  • More goods relative to demand brings prices down.
examples.answer: By importing scarce goods, releasing buffer stocks and curbing hoarding — more supply relative to demand lowers prices.

recap:
• Monetary measures (RBI): raise repo/CRR/SLR, sell securities → tighten credit.
  • Fiscal measures (government): cut spending, raise taxes, reduce deficit → lower demand.
  • Supply-side/administrative: import goods, release buffer stocks, curb hoarding, PDS & price controls.
  • Cure fits the cause: demand-pull → cut demand; cost-push → ease costs/raise supply.

quiz.q: To control inflation, the RBI would:
options: Raise the repo rate and CRR
quiz.explanation: Tighter monetary policy (higher repo/CRR) reduces credit and demand.

quiz.q: Releasing buffer stocks of food to control inflation is a:
quiz.explanation: Increasing supply (buffer stocks) is a supply-side measure.

questions.q: Inflation is a sustained rise in the:
questions.explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level.

questions.q: Inflation reduces the ____ of money.
questions.explanation: Inflation lowers the purchasing power of money.

questions.q: A slow, mild rise in prices is:
questions.explanation: A mild, slow rise is creeping inflation.

questions.q: An extremely rapid, out-of-control price rise is:
questions.explanation: An out-of-control rise is hyperinflation.

questions.q: A sustained fall in the general price level is:
questions.explanation: A falling price level is deflation.

questions.q: High inflation together with stagnation/unemployment is:
questions.explanation: Inflation plus stagnation is stagflation.

questions.q: 'Too much money chasing too few goods' is:
questions.explanation: Excess demand causing inflation is demand-pull.

questions.q: Inflation caused by rising input costs (wages, oil) is:
questions.explanation: Rising costs cause cost-push inflation.

questions.q: During inflation, who generally loses?
questions.explanation: Fixed-income earners and lenders lose to inflation.

questions.q: During inflation, who generally gains?
questions.explanation: Borrowers gain by repaying in cheaper money.

questions.q: To control inflation, the RBI would raise the:
questions.explanation: Raising the repo rate and CRR tightens credit.

questions.q: A fiscal measure to control inflation is to:
options: Cut public spending and raise taxes
questions.explanation: Less spending and higher taxes reduce demand.

questions.q: Releasing buffer stocks of food is a ____ measure.
questions.explanation: Raising supply via buffer stocks is a supply-side measure.

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is best fought by:
questions.explanation: Reducing demand cools demand-pull inflation.

questions.q: Disinflation means the inflation rate is:
questions.explanation: Disinflation is a slowing of the inflation rate.

questions.q: After a sharp rise in global crude-oil prices, transport and production costs climb and the price level rises. This is:
questions.explanation: Higher input (oil) costs push up prices regardless of demand — cost-push inflation.

questions.q: A retired person on a fixed pension finds it harder to manage during inflation because:
options: Their fixed income buys fewer goods as prices rise
questions.explanation: Fixed money income with rising prices means falling real income — a classic loser from inflation.

questions.q: A businessman who borrowed heavily before a period of high inflation effectively benefits because the loan is repaid in money that is:
options: Worth less than when it was borrowed
questions.explanation: Inflation erodes the real value of the fixed debt, so borrowers gain at lenders' expense.

questions.q: To fight clear demand-pull inflation, the most appropriate combination is:
options: Tight monetary policy plus contractionary fiscal policy
Lower taxes and lower repo rate
questions.explanation: Reducing both credit and government demand directly attacks the excess demand causing the inflation.

questions.q: Mild creeping inflation is sometimes seen as helpful because it can:
options: Encourage producers to invest and produce more
questions.explanation: A gentle, predictable rise in prices can raise expected profits and encourage production and investment.

questions.q: A government importing onions and releasing wheat from buffer stocks during a price spike is using:
questions.explanation: Adding to the supply of scarce goods directly eases their prices — a supply-side anti-inflation measure.

questions.q: Why can cost-push inflation be harder to cure with tight monetary policy alone?
options: It comes from supply costs, not excess demand, so cutting demand may just cause unemployment
questions.explanation: Squeezing demand does not lower input costs, and may slow output (risking stagflation), so supply-side action is also needed.

questions.q: Holding gold and land during high inflation tends to protect wealth because their value:
options: Rises with the general price level (real assets)
questions.explanation: Real assets keep pace with inflation, unlike cash whose purchasing power erodes.

questions.q: The Reserve Bank's main goal in setting interest rates is usually described as keeping inflation:
questions.explanation: Modern central banks aim for low, stable inflation to support steady growth and protect purchasing power.

questions.q: Inflation 'redistributes' income, which means it:
options: Shifts real income from some groups (lenders, fixed-income earners) to others (borrowers, traders)
questions.explanation: Because it hits groups unevenly, inflation transfers real purchasing power from losers to gainers.
